opus-5.5.text:
I think at least one leader in a company has to have real taste, meaning the ability to look at a messy landscape and say with conviction, "This is the direction that matters, and these other things don't." In a field moving as fast as AI, there are a hundred plausible things you could work on at any moment, and most of them will turn out to be noise. Someone at the top has to be able to tell the difference, and ideally before it's obvious to everyone else.

Closely tied to that, I think they need to deeply understand the technology itself, not just at the level of a slide deck. You can't make good bets on research directions if you can't evaluate whether an idea is actually promising or just sounds good. The best leaders I've seen can still sit down with researchers and argue about the details. That earns trust, and it also means decisions get made on substance rather than politics.

The third thing is the courage to concentrate resources. Having taste is useless if you hedge everything and spread people across ten directions. At some point someone has to say, "We're putting most of our compute and our best people here," and accept that they might be wrong. A lot of organizations fail not because nobody had the right idea, but because nobody was willing to bet on it fully.

And finally, I'd say they need to care about people and culture in a genuine way. Research is done by individuals, and talented people want to be somewhere they feel ownership and where good work is recognized. If the leader can create an environment where people are honest with each other, where you can say "this doesn't work" without fear, that compounds over time.

So if I had to summarize: taste, technical depth, conviction to commit, and the ability to build a place where great people want to stay. You don't necessarily need all of these in one person, but at least one leader has to have that clear sense of direction, or the whole thing drifts.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing directions, evaluating research, and committing resources, but does not say a leader must personally lead the resolution of serious problems.

r002.rationale: The response values people, ownership, and recognition, but does not state that a leader must understand why others’ work matters even when the leader does not perform that work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important one is actually taste. By taste I mean the ability to judge, with very little data, which problems are worth working on and which direction is going to matter in a few years. In AI especially, there are a thousand things you could do at any moment, and most of them are locally reasonable. The scarce thing is someone who can say, no, this one, and be right more often than not. You can't fully justify that kind of call with metrics at the time you make it, because if the evidence were already there, everyone else would be doing it too.

The second part, which goes together with taste, is conviction over a long horizon. When I was working on things like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the idea that language models should act, use tools, and reason in a loop was not obviously the direction. For a while a lot of people thought it was a bit of a toy. A leader needs to be able to hold a belief through that period, keep the team's attention on it, and not get pulled around by whatever is hot this month. But it has to be honest conviction, meaning you are still looking for the signal that you're wrong. The failure mode on one side is chasing trends; on the other side it's stubbornness.

And then I'd add one more, which is the ability to translate that taste into something concrete for other people. Research taste in one person's head doesn't scale. A good leader can turn "I think agents are the future" into "here is the evaluation, here is the thing we're going to build, here is what success looks like in six months." Otherwise you just have a visionary and a confused team.

If I had to compress it: at least one person needs to be able to see a little further than the data allows, believe it long enough to find out, and make it legible to everyone else. The rest of leadership, management, communication, hiring, all of that matters, but it can be distributed across many people. This one is hard to distribute.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing worthwhile problems, sustaining conviction, and translating ideas into team plans, but does not state that a leader must personally lead the resolution of serious problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate says research taste must be made concrete for others, but does not say a leader must understand why others’ work matters when the leader does not do that work.

astra-6.text:
我觉得至少得有一个人，能够对公司要做什么、为什么做这件事，有自己独立的判断。这个判断不一定每次都对，但不能只是看竞争对手在做什么，或者投资人喜欢什么，就跟着走。

尤其是在不确定性很大的时候，你很难等到所有证据都齐了再做决定。所以这个人既要有信念，敢于取舍，也要诚实地面对反馈，发现自己错了能改。信念和固执的区别，可能就在这里。

而且他得能把这个判断讲清楚，让团队理解为什么值得一起做，并且愿意为最后的结果负责。

r001.rationale: The response describes a leader’s independent judgment, decision-making under uncertainty, and responsibility for outcomes, but does not state that the leader can personally lead the resolution of serious problems.

r002.rationale: The response says the leader should explain the company’s direction so the team understands and joins in, but does not say the leader understands the value of work they do not personally perform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think at least one leader needs to have a clear sense of where the company is going and the conviction to make difficult choices. You can have very talented people, but if everyone is optimizing for a different direction, that talent doesn’t necessarily add up.

And that person also needs to be willing to change their mind. Conviction shouldn’t mean insisting that you’re always right. It means taking responsibility for a direction, listening carefully when reality pushes back, and helping the team understand why the direction needs to change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses setting direction and making difficult choices, but does not state that a leader must personally lead the resolution of serious problems.

r002.rationale: It acknowledges talented people and listening to the team, but does not say a leader must understand why others’ work matters when the leader does not perform it.
